{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q634195]] Wikidata name: onryō [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 08:49, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{short description|Type of ghost in Japanese folklore}} {{for|the Japanese professional wrestler|Onryo (wrestler)}} {{Jmyth infobox}} {{Italic title}} [[File:Yoshitsuya The Lightning Bolt.jpg|thumb|{{transliteration|ja|[[Ukiyo-e]]}} by [[:en:Utagawa Yoshitsuya|Utagawa Yoshitsuya]] depicts the moment when [[:en:Emperor Sutoku|Emperor Sutoku]], who died in exile, became an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.]] [[File:Taira no Masakado Kubizuka.jpg|thumb|The headstone of [[:en:Taira no Masakado|Taira no Masakado]], located between the skyscrapers of [[:en:Ōtemachi|Ōtemachi]] near [[:en:Tokyo Station|Tokyo Station]], was renovated in 2021 when the surrounding skyscrapers were rebuilt, but the headstone was never moved.]] [[File:Tsukioka (Taiso) Yoshitoshi (1839-1892), Sugawara no Michizane roept een onweersbui op boven KyotoKôkoku (1880).jpg|thumb|{{transliteration|ja|Ukiyo-e}} by [[:en:Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]] depicting [[:en:Sugawara no Michizane|Sugawara no Michizane]] as the {{nihongo3|{{transliteration|ja|[[kami]]}} of thunder||[[:en:Tenjin (kami)|Tenjin]]}}. After Sugawara no Michizane's death, lightning struck the palace, killing and injuring many of the powerful people involved in his banishment, and Sugawara no Michizane was enshrined in the {{transliteration|ja|[[Tenmangū]]}} ([[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]]) as the Tenjin.]] [[File:Hokusai Onryo.jpg|thumb|Onryō from the {{nihongo||近世怪談霜夜星|Kinsei-Kaidan-Shimoyonohoshi}}]]
In Japanese traditional beliefs and literature, {{nihongo3|{{lit|[[:en:Vengeful ghost|vengeful spirit]]}}, sometimes rendered "wrathful spirits", "hatred spirits", "resentful spirits", "ruthless spirits", "envious spirits", "dark spirits", "fallen spirits", or "downcast spirits"||'''onryō'''}}<ref name="grappard"/> are a type of ghost ({{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Yūrei|Yūrei]]}}) believed to be capable of causing harm in the world of the living, injuring or killing enemies, or even causing natural disasters to exact [[:en:revenge|vengeance]] to "redress" the wrongs it received while alive, then taking their spirits from their dying bodies. {{transliteration|ja|Onryō}} are often depicted as wronged women, who are traumatized, envious, disappointed, bitter, or just infuriated by what happened during life and exact revenge in death. These kinds of ghosts appear extremely vengeful, ruthless, heartless, brutal, cruel, deranged, egotistical, selfish, bloodthirsty, and cold-hearted.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lovelace |first=Ada |date=2008 |title=Ghostly and monstrous manifestations of women: Edo to contemporary |url=https://irishgothicjournal.net/issue5 |journal=The Irish Journal of Gothic and Horror Studies |issue=5 |page=30}}</ref>
[[:en:Emperor Sutoku|Emperor Sutoku]], [[:en:Taira no Masakado|Taira no Masakado]], and [[:en:Sugawara no Michizane|Sugawara no Michizane]] are called the {{nihongo|Three Great Onryō of Japan|[[:ja:日本三大怨霊|日本三大怨霊]]|Nihon Sandai Onryō}} because they are considered to be the most powerful and revered {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} in Japanese history. After they died with resentment and anger, there was a series of deaths of political opponents, natural disasters, and wars, and the rulers enshrined them as {{transliteration|ja|[[kami]]}} and deified them in [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] to appease the resentment and anger that had turned them into {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://dot.asahi.com/dot/2019091300037.html?page=1|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210304044436/https://dot.asahi.com/dot/2019091300037.html?page=1|script-title=ja:崇徳天皇はなぜ「日本三大怨霊」の一人になったのか？ 悲劇の人生とは|language=ja|publisher=[[Asahi Shimbun]]|date=14 September 2019|archive-date=4 March 2021|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://thegate12.com/jp/article/351|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221103100624/https://thegate12.com/jp/article/351|script-title=ja:史上最恐！【日本三大怨霊】にまつわる悲しい歴史とは？ゆかりの場所も紹介|language=ja|publisher=The Gate|date=22 January 2021|archive-date=3 November 2022|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref>
{{transliteration|ja|Onryō}} are used as subjects in various traditional Japanese performing arts such as [[:en:Noh|Noh]], [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]], and [[Rakugo]]; for example, {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Hannya|Hannya]]}} is a Noh mask representing a female {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.<ref name="kurabayashi">{{cite book|pages=6, 7, 39|title=般若面を打つ 原寸型紙と詳細なプロセス写真で学ぶ|author=Akira Kurabayashi|publisher=Japan Publications, Inc.|year=2013|isbn=978-4817050823}}</ref>
The Japanese people's reverence for {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} has been passed down to the present day. {{nihongo|The head mound of Taira no Masakado|[[:ja:将門塚|将門塚]]|Masakado-zuka or Shōmon-zuka}}, located between skyscrapers near [[:en:Tokyo Station|Tokyo Station]], was to be moved several times as part of urban redevelopment projects, but each move resulted in the death of a construction worker and a series of accidents. Although the buildings surrounding the Taira no Masakado mound have been rebuilt many times, the mound has remained intact between the high-rise buildings. Even today, the mound is carefully maintained.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://president.jp/articles/-/37926?page=2|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210928235755/https://president.jp/articles/-/37926?page=2|script-title=ja:地価40億円の超一等地｢Taira no Masakadoの首塚｣が再開発を免れているホラーな理由|language=ja|publisher=President Online|date=14 August 2022|archive-date=28 September 2021|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref>
The term {{nihongo||[[Wiktionary:御霊|御霊]]|[[goryō]]}} is often used as a synonym for {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}, but the term {{transliteration|ja|goryō}} is more commonly used to refer to the {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} that have become the object of the people's reverence after a noble person has died a politically unjust death. {{nihongo3||[[:ja:御霊信仰|御霊信仰]]|Goryō Shinko}} refers to the belief that the {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} of people who have died unfortunate deaths cause hauntings and disasters, and the belief that they are enshrined as {{transliteration|ja|kami}} to appease them.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%BE%A1%E9%9C%8A%E4%BF%A1%E4%BB%B0-66557|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230206025148/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%BE%A1%E9%9C%8A%E4%BF%A1%E4%BB%B0-66557|script-title=ja:御霊信仰|language=ja|publisher=Kotobank|archive-date=6 February 2023|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%BE%A1%E9%9C%8A-505236|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230206025142/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%BE%A1%E9%9C%8A-505236|script-title=ja:御霊|language=ja|publisher=Kotobank|archive-date=6 February 2023|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%80%A8%E9%9C%8A-42048|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230206025148/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%80%A8%E9%9C%8A-42048|script-title=ja:怨霊|language=ja|publisher=Kotobank|archive-date=6 February 2023|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref>
==Origin== While the origin of {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} is unclear, belief in their existence can be traced back to the 8th century and was based on the idea that powerful and enraged souls of the dead could influence, harm, and kill the living. The earliest {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} cult that developed was around [[:en:Prince Naga|Prince Naga]] who died in 729;<ref name="grappard"/> and the first record of possession by the {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} spirit affecting health is found in the chronicle {{transliteration|ja|[[Shoku Nihongi]]}} (797), which states that "{{nihongo|[[Fujiwara Hirotsugu]]|[[:ja:藤原広嗣|藤原広嗣]]}}'s soul harmed [[:en:Genbō|Genbō]] to death" (Hirotsugu having died in a failed insurrection, named the "[[:en:Fujiwara no Hirotsugu Rebellion|Fujiwara no Hirotsugu Rebellion]]", after failing to remove his rival, the priest Genbō, from power).<ref>{{Harvnb|Suzuki|2011|loc=135 (note 2 to Chapter 2)}}</ref><ref>{{Harvnb|McCullough|1973|p=97}}</ref>
==Vengeance== According to the belief of [[:en:Ikiryō|Ikiryō]], a person's soul or spirit exists naturally when it is stable or in balance. When too much hatred or resentment brews, it can become separated from the body, resulting in the spirit becoming an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}. This can allegedly also occur in individuals who died an untimely death.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Yamada |first1=Yuji |title=怨霊とは何か (What is [an] Onryo) |publisher=Chuokoron-Shinsha |location=Japan |url=https://www.kinokuniya.co.jp/f/dsg-01-9784121022813}}</ref>
Traditionally in Japan, {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} driven by [[:en:revenge|vengeance]] were thought capable of causing not only their enemy's death, as in the case of Hirotsugu's vengeful spirit held responsible for killing the priest [[:en:Genbō|Genbō]],<ref>{{citation|last=McCullough|first=William H.|title=Spirit Possession in the Heian Period|editor-last1=Ōta|editor-first1=Saburo (太田三郎)|editor-last2=Fukuda|editor-first2=Rikutaro (福田陸太郎)|journal=Studies on Japanese Culture (日本文化研究論集)|volume=1|year=1973|page=97|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qLAdAQAAMAAJ}}; (Also printed in ''Nihon Bunka Kenkyū Kokusai Kaigi gijiroku'' (日本文化研究国際会議議事錄) ([https://books.google.com/books?id=RN9YAAAAMAAJ Volume 1, 1973], pp. 350- (p.356)</ref> but causing natural disasters such as [[:en:Earthquake|Earthquake]]s, [[:en:Fire|Fire]]s, [[:en:Storm|Storm]]s, [[:en:Drought|Drought]], [[:en:Famine|Famine]] and [[:en:Pandemic|pestilence]],<ref name="grappard"/> as in the case of [[:en:Prince Sawara|Prince Sawara]]'s spirit embittered against his brother, the [[Emperor Kanmu]].<ref name="suzuki">{{cite book|last=Suzuki|first=Yui|title=Medicine Master Buddha: The Iconic Worship of Yakushi in Heian Japan|publisher=BRILL|year=2011|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dgo7JV9vNCQC&pg=PA29|pages=29–31|isbn=978-9004196018}}</ref> In common parlance, such vengeance exacted by supernatural beings or forces is termed {{nihongo||[[:ja:祟り|祟り]]|tatari}}.<ref name="grappard">{{citation|last=Grappard|first=Allan G.|contribution=Religious practices|editor-last=Hall|editor-first=John Whitney|volume=2|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eiTWWfoyuyAC&pg=PA560|pages=559–|isbn=978-0521223539|title=The Cambridge History of Japan|year=1988|publisher=Cambridge University Press }}</ref>
The [[Emperor Kanmu]] had accused his brother Sawara, possibly falsely, of plotting to remove him from the throne. Sawara was then exiled, and died by fasting. According to a number of scholars, the reason that the Emperor moved the capital to [[Nagaoka-kyō]] thence to [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]] was an attempt to avoid the wrath of his brother's spirit, according to a number of scholars.<ref name="suzuki"/> This not succeeding entirely, the emperor tried to lift the curse by appeasing his brother's ghost, by performing Buddhist rites to pay respect, and granting Prince Sawara the posthumous title of emperor.<ref name="suzuki"/>
A well-known example of appeasement of the {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} spirit is the case of [[:en:Sugawara no Michizane|Sugawara no Michizane]], who had been politically disgraced and died in exile. It was believed to cause the death of his calumniators in quick succession, as well as catastrophes (especially lightning damage), and the court tried to appease the wrathful spirit by restoring Michizane's old Rank and position.<ref name="grappard"/> Michizane became deified in the cult of the [[:en:Tenjin (kami)|Tenjin]], with [[Tenmangū|Tenman-gū]] shrines erected around him.
===Examples=== Possibly the most famous {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} is Oiwa, from the {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Yotsuya Kaidan|Yotsuya Kaidan]]}}. In this story the husband remains unharmed; however, he is the target of the {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}'s vengeance. Oiwa's vengeance on him is not physical retribution, but rather psychological torment.
Other examples include:
; How a Man's Wife Became a Vengeful Ghost and How Her Malignity Was Diverted by a Master of Divination : In this tale from the medieval collection {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Konjaku Monogatarishū|Konjaku Monogatarishū]]}}, an abandoned wife is found dead with a full head of hair intact and her bones still attached. The husband, fearing retribution from her spirit, asks a [[Onmyōji|diviner]] for aid. The husband must endure while grabbing her hair and riding astride her corpse. She complains of the heavy load and leaves the house to "go looking" (presumably for her husband), but after a day she gives up and returns, after which the diviner is able to complete her exorcism with an incantation.<ref>{{cite book|translator-last=Jones|translator-first=S. W.|title=Ages ago; thirty-seven tales from the Konjaku monogatari collection|publisher=[[Harvard University Press]]|location=Cambridge, Massachusetts|year=1959|page=72|isbn=9780674181366 |format=snippet|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nv-wAAAAIAAJ}}</ref><ref>One of the texts cited by Jones: {{citation|editor-last=Haga|editor-first=Yaichi (芳賀矢一)|script-chapter=ja:卷第廿四/第20: 人妻成悪靈除其害陰陽師語 |script-title=ja:攷証今昔物語集 |title=Kōshō konjaku monogatari shū |volume=3 |year=1921 |page=106 |url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/945416}}</ref> ; Of a Promise Broken : In this tale from the [[:en:Izumo Province|Izumo]] area recorded by [[:en:Lafcadio Hearn|Lafcadio Hearn]], a [[:en:Samurai|Samurai]] vows to his dying wife never to remarry. He soon breaks this promise, and the ghost of the deceased wife murders her husband's new young bride, ripping her head off. A watchman chases down the apparition, and, while slashing his sword, recites a [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] prayer, destroying the ghost of the dead wife.<ref>{{citation|last=Hearn|first=Lafcadio|chapter=Of a Promise Broken|publisher=Little, Brown|year=1901|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DGEiAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA15|pages=15–26|title=A Japanese miscellany}}</ref>
==In media==
The {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} is a staple of the [[:en:J-Horror|J-Horror genre]], most notable being [[:en:Sadako Yamamura|Sadako Yamamura]] and [[:en:Kayako Saeki|Kayako Saeki]] from the ''[[:en:The Ring (franchise)|Ring]]'' and ''[[:en:Ju-On (franchise)|Ju-On]]'' franchises, respectively. The characters in these works are almost exclusively women who were wronged in life and returned as {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} to wreak havoc on the living and obtain revenge.<ref>{{Cite web|last=O'Sullivan|first=Dan|date=2020-10-27|title=Japan's Onryō Spirits Inhabit a Purgatory of Revenge and Cosmic Rage|url=http://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/monster-mythology-onryo|access-date=2021-05-04|website=Atlas Obscura|language=en}}</ref>
In ''[[:en:The Ring (franchise)|The Ring]]'' [[:en:Sadako Yamamura|Sadako Yamamura]] is the main antagonist. Her origin is from the ''Ring'' novel series by [[:en:Koji Suzuki|Koji Suzuki]], where she haunts and kills people through tapes on a TV. Before her death she is raped by a doctor with smallpox, who seals her in a well where she dies. Before Sadako dies she promises to take revenge on the world, and becomes an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.
The aforementioned {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Yotsuya Kaidan|Yotsuya Kaidan]]}} has been made into numerous movies and retold many times over the course of Japanese history. The story revolves around Tamiya Iemon and his wife Oiwa. Their relationship is not a happy one, and through some set of circumstances Iemon gives Oiwa a powder that permanently disfigures her face. Upon realizing this Oiwa takes her own life and that of her baby. After her death she comes back to haunt Iemon and his new wife, becoming an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.<ref>{{Cite book |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JR9JAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA168 |chapter=Epic Yotsuya Ghost Tale |author=Tsuruya Nanboku IV |title=An Edo Anthology: Literature from Japan's Mega-City, 1750-1850 |orig-date=1825 |date=2013 |publisher=[[University of Hawaiʻi Press]] |editor1=Sumie Jones |editor2=Kenji Watanabe |isbn=978-0-8248-3776-1 |oclc=859157616 |pages=168–182}}</ref>
{{transliteration|ja|[[Banchō Sarayashiki]]}} is another Japanese ghost story that has been retold many ways. In this story Okiku, a beautiful maid, is the target of desire for the samurai whose house she works at, Aoyama Tessan. She continually refuses his advances, and in a fit of rage Tessan hides one of 10 expensive plates that Okiku is in charge of counting. When Okiku cannot find the 10th plate she recounts them obsessively, panicking more each time. Tessan tells her he will forgive her losing the plate if she becomes his mistress, but even then she refuses him. At her refusal Tessan throws her into a well on the property, where she dies. After this, every night Okiku rises from the well, softly counting to 9, and then letting out a horrendous shriek once she reaches 10. She has become an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Kaidan of Bancho Sarayashiki The Dish Mansion at Bancho |url=https://www.grimoireofhorror.com/the-yurei/kaidan-bancho-sarayashiki/ |access-date=2022-04-11 |website=Grimoire of Horror |date=11 January 2021 |language=en-US}}</ref>
{{nihongo|[[List of Killer Instinct characters#Hisako|Hisako]]|久子||extra= "Eternal Child" or "Everlasting Child"}}, from the third entry of the fighting game ''[[:en:Killer Instinct|Killer Instinct]]'', is an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} who died while defending her village. She still haunts her old village and will take vengeance on anyone who desecrates its ruins with her {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Naginata|Naginata]]}}. She has pale white skin and long black hair like most {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ultra-combo.com/characters/hisako/|title = Hisako|date = 12 December 2016}}</ref>
In 2018, the asymmetrical horror game ''[[:en:Dead by Daylight|Dead by Daylight]]'' released the ''Shattered Bloodline'' chapter DLC, and with it came Rin Yamaoka, The Spirit. The Spirit is an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} who returns from the dead after being brutally murdered by her father.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Shattered Bloodline - Dead by Daylight|url=http://deadbydaylight.com/en/chapters/shattered-bloodline|access-date=2021-05-04|website=deadbydaylight.com|language=en}}</ref> In March 2022, Sadako Yamamura was added as a playable character.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sea.ign.com/dead-by-daylight/182036/news/dead-by-daylight-x-ringu-crossover-revealed|title = Dead by Daylight x Ringu Crossover Revealed|date = 15 February 2022}}</ref>
The term {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} is also present in the game ''[[:en:Phasmophobia (video game)|Phasmophobia]]''. It is one of 24 ghost types that the player can identify, and is noted for treating lit candles like a crucifix.
Yoshie Kimura, the main antagonist from ''[[Death Forest]]'', is an Onryō. She died when exploring the forest with her classmate, from being beaten to death by an unknown person.
Mizu, the protagonist of the 2023 [[:en:Netflix|Netflix]] series ''[[:en:Blue Eye Samurai|Blue Eye Samurai]]'' shares many similarities with, and is often compared diegetically to, an Onryō.
==Physical appearance== Traditionally, {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} and other {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Yūrei|Yūrei]]}} (ghosts) had no particular appearance. However, with the rising of popularity of [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], a specific [[:en:costume|costume]] was developed.
Highly visual in nature, and with a single actor often assuming various roles within a play, kabuki developed a system of visual shorthand that allowed the audience to instantly clue in as to which character is on stage, as well as emphasize the emotions and expressions of the actor.
A ghost costume consisted of three main elements: * {{nihongo|White burial [[:en:Kimono|Kimono]]|[[:ja:白装束|白装束]]|shiro-shōzoku}} or {{nihongo||[[:ja:死に装束|死に装束]]|shini-shōzoku}}. This garment was also worn during {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Seppuku|Seppuku]]}}. *Wild, unkempt long black hair that often hides their face until they choose to reveal it. *Face make-up consisting of {{nihongo|white foundation||[[:en:oshiroi|oshiroi]]}} coupled with dramatic face painting ({{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Kumadori|Kumadori]]}}) of {{nihongo|blue shadows|藍隈|aiguma|extra2="[[:en:Indigo|Indigo]] fringe"}}, much like villains are depicted in kabuki make-up artistry.<ref>{{cite book|author=日本博学倶楽部|title=「通」になれる古典芸能を楽しむ本: 落語・歌舞伎から能・狂言まで|publisher=PHP研究所|year=2005|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZpY2LFHGK34C&pg=PT57|page=57|isbn=978-4569665498}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Parker|first=Helen S. E.|title=Progressive Traditions: An Illustrated Study of Plot Repetition In Traditional Japanese Theatre|publisher=BRILL|year=2006|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=L3pp4I-eoZIC&pg=PA87|page=87|isbn=978-9004145344}}</ref>{{efn|In addition to blue, {{nihongo|brown shadows|代赭隈|taishaguma|extra2="[[:en:red ochre|red ochre]] fringe"}} or black {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Kumadori|Kumadori]]}} ({{Harvnb|日本博学倶楽部|2005|p=57}}) are also used.}}

{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q634195]] Wikidata name: onryō [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 08:49, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{short description|Type of ghost in Japanese folklore}} {{for|the Japanese professional wrestler|Onryo (wrestler)}} {{Jmyth infobox}} {{Italic title}} [[File:Yoshitsuya The Lightning Bolt.jpg|thumb|{{transliteration|ja|[[Ukiyo-e]]}} by [[:en:Utagawa Yoshitsuya|Utagawa Yoshitsuya]] depicts the moment when [[:en:Emperor Sutoku|Emperor Sutoku]], who died in exile, became an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.]] [[File:Taira no Masakado Kubizuka.jpg|thumb|The headstone of [[:en:Taira no Masakado|Taira no Masakado]], located between the skyscrapers of [[:en:Ōtemachi|Ōtemachi]] near [[:en:Tokyo Station|Tokyo Station]], was renovated in 2021 when the surrounding skyscrapers were rebuilt, but the headstone was never moved.]] [[File:Tsukioka (Taiso) Yoshitoshi (1839-1892), Sugawara no Michizane roept een onweersbui op boven KyotoKôkoku (1880).jpg|thumb|{{transliteration|ja|Ukiyo-e}} by [[:en:Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]] depicting [[:en:Sugawara no Michizane|Sugawara no Michizane]] as the {{nihongo3|{{transliteration|ja|[[kami]]}} of thunder||[[:en:Tenjin (kami)|Tenjin]]}}. After Sugawara no Michizane's death, lightning struck the palace, killing and injuring many of the powerful people involved in his banishment, and Sugawara no Michizane was enshrined in the {{transliteration|ja|[[Tenmangū]]}} ([[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]]) as the Tenjin.]] [[File:Hokusai Onryo.jpg|thumb|Onryō from the {{nihongo||近世怪談霜夜星|Kinsei-Kaidan-Shimoyonohoshi}}]]
In Japanese traditional beliefs and literature, {{nihongo3|{{lit|[[:en:Vengeful ghost|vengeful spirit]]}}, sometimes rendered "wrathful spirits", "hatred spirits", "resentful spirits", "ruthless spirits", "envious spirits", "dark spirits", "fallen spirits", or "downcast spirits"||'''onryō'''}}<ref name="grappard"/> are a type of ghost ({{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Yūrei|Yūrei]]}}) believed to be capable of causing harm in the world of the living, injuring or killing enemies, or even causing natural disasters to exact [[:en:revenge|vengeance]] to "redress" the wrongs it received while alive, then taking their spirits from their dying bodies. {{transliteration|ja|Onryō}} are often depicted as wronged women, who are traumatized, envious, disappointed, bitter, or just infuriated by what happened during life and exact revenge in death. These kinds of ghosts appear extremely vengeful, ruthless, heartless, brutal, cruel, deranged, egotistical, selfish, bloodthirsty, and cold-hearted.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lovelace |first=Ada |date=2008 |title=Ghostly and monstrous manifestations of women: Edo to contemporary |url=https://irishgothicjournal.net/issue5 |journal=The Irish Journal of Gothic and Horror Studies |issue=5 |page=30}}</ref>
[[:en:Emperor Sutoku|Emperor Sutoku]], [[:en:Taira no Masakado|Taira no Masakado]], and [[:en:Sugawara no Michizane|Sugawara no Michizane]] are called the {{nihongo|Three Great Onryō of Japan|[[:ja:日本三大怨霊|日本三大怨霊]]|Nihon Sandai Onryō}} because they are considered to be the most powerful and revered {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} in Japanese history. After they died with resentment and anger, there was a series of deaths of political opponents, natural disasters, and wars, and the rulers enshrined them as {{transliteration|ja|[[kami]]}} and deified them in [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] to appease the resentment and anger that had turned them into {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://dot.asahi.com/dot/2019091300037.html?page=1|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210304044436/https://dot.asahi.com/dot/2019091300037.html?page=1|script-title=ja:崇徳天皇はなぜ「日本三大怨霊」の一人になったのか？ 悲劇の人生とは|language=ja|publisher=[[Asahi Shimbun]]|date=14 September 2019|archive-date=4 March 2021|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://thegate12.com/jp/article/351|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221103100624/https://thegate12.com/jp/article/351|script-title=ja:史上最恐！【日本三大怨霊】にまつわる悲しい歴史とは？ゆかりの場所も紹介|language=ja|publisher=The Gate|date=22 January 2021|archive-date=3 November 2022|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref>
{{transliteration|ja|Onryō}} are used as subjects in various traditional Japanese performing arts such as [[:en:Noh|Noh]], [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]], and [[Rakugo]]; for example, {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Hannya|Hannya]]}} is a Noh mask representing a female {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.<ref name="kurabayashi">{{cite book|pages=6, 7, 39|title=般若面を打つ 原寸型紙と詳細なプロセス写真で学ぶ|author=Akira Kurabayashi|publisher=Japan Publications, Inc.|year=2013|isbn=978-4817050823}}</ref>
The Japanese people's reverence for {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} has been passed down to the present day. {{nihongo|The head mound of Taira no Masakado|[[:ja:将門塚|将門塚]]|Masakado-zuka or Shōmon-zuka}}, located between skyscrapers near [[:en:Tokyo Station|Tokyo Station]], was to be moved several times as part of urban redevelopment projects, but each move resulted in the death of a construction worker and a series of accidents. Although the buildings surrounding the Taira no Masakado mound have been rebuilt many times, the mound has remained intact between the high-rise buildings. Even today, the mound is carefully maintained.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://president.jp/articles/-/37926?page=2|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210928235755/https://president.jp/articles/-/37926?page=2|script-title=ja:地価40億円の超一等地｢Taira no Masakadoの首塚｣が再開発を免れているホラーな理由|language=ja|publisher=President Online|date=14 August 2022|archive-date=28 September 2021|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref>
The term {{nihongo||[[Wiktionary:御霊|御霊]]|[[goryō]]}} is often used as a synonym for {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}, but the term {{transliteration|ja|goryō}} is more commonly used to refer to the {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} that have become the object of the people's reverence after a noble person has died a politically unjust death. {{nihongo3||[[:ja:御霊信仰|御霊信仰]]|Goryō Shinko}} refers to the belief that the {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} of people who have died unfortunate deaths cause hauntings and disasters, and the belief that they are enshrined as {{transliteration|ja|kami}} to appease them.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%BE%A1%E9%9C%8A%E4%BF%A1%E4%BB%B0-66557|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230206025148/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%BE%A1%E9%9C%8A%E4%BF%A1%E4%BB%B0-66557|script-title=ja:御霊信仰|language=ja|publisher=Kotobank|archive-date=6 February 2023|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%BE%A1%E9%9C%8A-505236|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230206025142/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%BE%A1%E9%9C%8A-505236|script-title=ja:御霊|language=ja|publisher=Kotobank|archive-date=6 February 2023|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%80%A8%E9%9C%8A-42048|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230206025148/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%80%A8%E9%9C%8A-42048|script-title=ja:怨霊|language=ja|publisher=Kotobank|archive-date=6 February 2023|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref>
==Origin== While the origin of {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} is unclear, belief in their existence can be traced back to the 8th century and was based on the idea that powerful and enraged souls of the dead could influence, harm, and kill the living. The earliest {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} cult that developed was around [[:en:Prince Naga|Prince Naga]] who died in 729;<ref name="grappard"/> and the first record of possession by the {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} spirit affecting health is found in the chronicle {{transliteration|ja|[[Shoku Nihongi]]}} (797), which states that "{{nihongo|[[Fujiwara Hirotsugu]]|[[:ja:藤原広嗣|藤原広嗣]]}}'s soul harmed [[:en:Genbō|Genbō]] to death" (Hirotsugu having died in a failed insurrection, named the "[[:en:Fujiwara no Hirotsugu Rebellion|Fujiwara no Hirotsugu Rebellion]]", after failing to remove his rival, the priest Genbō, from power).<ref>{{Harvnb|Suzuki|2011|loc=135 (note 2 to Chapter 2)}}</ref><ref>{{Harvnb|McCullough|1973|p=97}}</ref>
==Vengeance== According to the belief of [[:en:Ikiryō|Ikiryō]], a person's soul or spirit exists naturally when it is stable or in balance. When too much hatred or resentment brews, it can become separated from the body, resulting in the spirit becoming an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}. This can allegedly also occur in individuals who died an untimely death.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Yamada |first1=Yuji |title=怨霊とは何か (What is [an] Onryo) |publisher=Chuokoron-Shinsha |location=Japan |url=https://www.kinokuniya.co.jp/f/dsg-01-9784121022813}}</ref>
Traditionally in Japan, {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} driven by [[:en:revenge|vengeance]] were thought capable of causing not only their enemy's death, as in the case of Hirotsugu's vengeful spirit held responsible for killing the priest [[:en:Genbō|Genbō]],<ref>{{citation|last=McCullough|first=William H.|title=Spirit Possession in the Heian Period|editor-last1=Ōta|editor-first1=Saburo (太田三郎)|editor-last2=Fukuda|editor-first2=Rikutaro (福田陸太郎)|journal=Studies on Japanese Culture (日本文化研究論集)|volume=1|year=1973|page=97|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qLAdAQAAMAAJ}}; (Also printed in ''Nihon Bunka Kenkyū Kokusai Kaigi gijiroku'' (日本文化研究国際会議議事錄) ([https://books.google.com/books?id=RN9YAAAAMAAJ Volume 1, 1973], pp. 350- (p.356)</ref> but causing natural disasters such as [[:en:Earthquake|Earthquake]]s, [[:en:Fire|Fire]]s, [[:en:Storm|Storm]]s, [[:en:Drought|Drought]], [[:en:Famine|Famine]] and [[:en:Pandemic|pestilence]],<ref name="grappard"/> as in the case of [[:en:Prince Sawara|Prince Sawara]]'s spirit embittered against his brother, the [[Emperor Kanmu]].<ref name="suzuki">{{cite book|last=Suzuki|first=Yui|title=Medicine Master Buddha: The Iconic Worship of Yakushi in Heian Japan|publisher=BRILL|year=2011|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dgo7JV9vNCQC&pg=PA29|pages=29–31|isbn=978-9004196018}}</ref> In common parlance, such vengeance exacted by supernatural beings or forces is termed {{nihongo||[[:ja:祟り|祟り]]|tatari}}.<ref name="grappard">{{citation|last=Grappard|first=Allan G.|contribution=Religious practices|editor-last=Hall|editor-first=John Whitney|volume=2|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eiTWWfoyuyAC&pg=PA560|pages=559–|isbn=978-0521223539|title=The Cambridge History of Japan|year=1988|publisher=Cambridge University Press }}</ref>
The [[Emperor Kanmu]] had accused his brother Sawara, possibly falsely, of plotting to remove him from the throne. Sawara was then exiled, and died by fasting. According to a number of scholars, the reason that the Emperor moved the capital to [[Nagaoka-kyō]] thence to [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]] was an attempt to avoid the wrath of his brother's spirit, according to a number of scholars.<ref name="suzuki"/> This not succeeding entirely, the emperor tried to lift the curse by appeasing his brother's ghost, by performing Buddhist rites to pay respect, and granting Prince Sawara the posthumous title of emperor.<ref name="suzuki"/>
A well-known example of appeasement of the {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} spirit is the case of [[:en:Sugawara no Michizane|Sugawara no Michizane]], who had been politically disgraced and died in exile. It was believed to cause the death of his calumniators in quick succession, as well as catastrophes (especially lightning damage), and the court tried to appease the wrathful spirit by restoring Michizane's old Rank and position.<ref name="grappard"/> Michizane became deified in the cult of the [[:en:Tenjin (kami)|Tenjin]], with [[Tenmangū|Tenman-gū]] shrines erected around him.
===Examples=== Possibly the most famous {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} is Oiwa, from the {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Yotsuya Kaidan|Yotsuya Kaidan]]}}. In this story the husband remains unharmed; however, he is the target of the {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}'s vengeance. Oiwa's vengeance on him is not physical retribution, but rather psychological torment.
Other examples include:
; How a Man's Wife Became a Vengeful Ghost and How Her Malignity Was Diverted by a Master of Divination : In this tale from the medieval collection {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Konjaku Monogatarishū|Konjaku Monogatarishū]]}}, an abandoned wife is found dead with a full head of hair intact and her bones still attached. The husband, fearing retribution from her spirit, asks a [[Onmyōji|diviner]] for aid. The husband must endure while grabbing her hair and riding astride her corpse. She complains of the heavy load and leaves the house to "go looking" (presumably for her husband), but after a day she gives up and returns, after which the diviner is able to complete her exorcism with an incantation.<ref>{{cite book|translator-last=Jones|translator-first=S. W.|title=Ages ago; thirty-seven tales from the Konjaku monogatari collection|publisher=[[Harvard University Press]]|location=Cambridge, Massachusetts|year=1959|page=72|isbn=9780674181366 |format=snippet|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nv-wAAAAIAAJ}}</ref><ref>One of the texts cited by Jones: {{citation|editor-last=Haga|editor-first=Yaichi (芳賀矢一)|script-chapter=ja:卷第廿四/第20: 人妻成悪靈除其害陰陽師語 |script-title=ja:攷証今昔物語集 |title=Kōshō konjaku monogatari shū |volume=3 |year=1921 |page=106 |url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/945416}}</ref> ; Of a Promise Broken : In this tale from the [[:en:Izumo Province|Izumo]] area recorded by [[:en:Lafcadio Hearn|Lafcadio Hearn]], a [[:en:Samurai|Samurai]] vows to his dying wife never to remarry. He soon breaks this promise, and the ghost of the deceased wife murders her husband's new young bride, ripping her head off. A watchman chases down the apparition, and, while slashing his sword, recites a [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] prayer, destroying the ghost of the dead wife.<ref>{{citation|last=Hearn|first=Lafcadio|chapter=Of a Promise Broken|publisher=Little, Brown|year=1901|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DGEiAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA15|pages=15–26|title=A Japanese miscellany}}</ref>
==In media==
The {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} is a staple of the [[:en:J-Horror|J-Horror genre]], most notable being [[:en:Sadako Yamamura|Sadako Yamamura]] and [[:en:Kayako Saeki|Kayako Saeki]] from the ''[[:en:The Ring (franchise)|Ring]]'' and ''[[:en:Ju-On (franchise)|Ju-On]]'' franchises, respectively. The characters in these works are almost exclusively women who were wronged in life and returned as {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} to wreak havoc on the living and obtain revenge.<ref>{{Cite web|last=O'Sullivan|first=Dan|date=2020-10-27|title=Japan's Onryō Spirits Inhabit a Purgatory of Revenge and Cosmic Rage|url=http://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/monster-mythology-onryo|access-date=2021-05-04|website=Atlas Obscura|language=en}}</ref>
In ''[[:en:The Ring (franchise)|The Ring]]'' [[:en:Sadako Yamamura|Sadako Yamamura]] is the main antagonist. Her origin is from the ''Ring'' novel series by [[:en:Koji Suzuki|Koji Suzuki]], where she haunts and kills people through tapes on a TV. Before her death she is raped by a doctor with smallpox, who seals her in a well where she dies. Before Sadako dies she promises to take revenge on the world, and becomes an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.
The aforementioned {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Yotsuya Kaidan|Yotsuya Kaidan]]}} has been made into numerous movies and retold many times over the course of Japanese history. The story revolves around Tamiya Iemon and his wife Oiwa. Their relationship is not a happy one, and through some set of circumstances Iemon gives Oiwa a powder that permanently disfigures her face. Upon realizing this Oiwa takes her own life and that of her baby. After her death she comes back to haunt Iemon and his new wife, becoming an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.<ref>{{Cite book |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JR9JAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA168 |chapter=Epic Yotsuya Ghost Tale |author=Tsuruya Nanboku IV |title=An Edo Anthology: Literature from Japan's Mega-City, 1750-1850 |orig-date=1825 |date=2013 |publisher=[[University of Hawaiʻi Press]] |editor1=Sumie Jones |editor2=Kenji Watanabe |isbn=978-0-8248-3776-1 |oclc=859157616 |pages=168–182}}</ref>
{{transliteration|ja|[[Banchō Sarayashiki]]}} is another Japanese ghost story that has been retold many ways. In this story Okiku, a beautiful maid, is the target of desire for the samurai whose house she works at, Aoyama Tessan. She continually refuses his advances, and in a fit of rage Tessan hides one of 10 expensive plates that Okiku is in charge of counting. When Okiku cannot find the 10th plate she recounts them obsessively, panicking more each time. Tessan tells her he will forgive her losing the plate if she becomes his mistress, but even then she refuses him. At her refusal Tessan throws her into a well on the property, where she dies. After this, every night Okiku rises from the well, softly counting to 9, and then letting out a horrendous shriek once she reaches 10. She has become an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Kaidan of Bancho Sarayashiki The Dish Mansion at Bancho |url=https://www.grimoireofhorror.com/the-yurei/kaidan-bancho-sarayashiki/ |access-date=2022-04-11 |website=Grimoire of Horror |date=11 January 2021 |language=en-US}}</ref>
{{nihongo|[[List of Killer Instinct characters#Hisako|Hisako]]|久子||extra= "Eternal Child" or "Everlasting Child"}}, from the third entry of the fighting game ''[[:en:Killer Instinct|Killer Instinct]]'', is an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} who died while defending her village. She still haunts her old village and will take vengeance on anyone who desecrates its ruins with her {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Naginata|Naginata]]}}. She has pale white skin and long black hair like most {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ultra-combo.com/characters/hisako/|title = Hisako|date = 12 December 2016}}</ref>
In 2018, the asymmetrical horror game ''[[:en:Dead by Daylight|Dead by Daylight]]'' released the ''Shattered Bloodline'' chapter DLC, and with it came Rin Yamaoka, The Spirit. The Spirit is an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} who returns from the dead after being brutally murdered by her father.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Shattered Bloodline - Dead by Daylight|url=http://deadbydaylight.com/en/chapters/shattered-bloodline|access-date=2021-05-04|website=deadbydaylight.com|language=en}}</ref> In March 2022, Sadako Yamamura was added as a playable character.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sea.ign.com/dead-by-daylight/182036/news/dead-by-daylight-x-ringu-crossover-revealed|title = Dead by Daylight x Ringu Crossover Revealed|date = 15 February 2022}}</ref>
The term {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} is also present in the game ''[[:en:Phasmophobia (video game)|Phasmophobia]]''. It is one of 24 ghost types that the player can identify, and is noted for treating lit candles like a crucifix.
Yoshie Kimura, the main antagonist from ''[[Death Forest]]'', is an Onryō. She died when exploring the forest with her classmate, from being beaten to death by an unknown person.
Mizu, the protagonist of the 2023 [[:en:Netflix|Netflix]] series ''[[:en:Blue Eye Samurai|Blue Eye Samurai]]'' shares many similarities with, and is often compared diegetically to, an Onryō.
==Physical appearance== Traditionally, {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} and other {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Yūrei|Yūrei]]}} (ghosts) had no particular appearance. However, with the rising of popularity of [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], a specific [[:en:costume|costume]] was developed.
Highly visual in nature, and with a single actor often assuming various roles within a play, kabuki developed a system of visual shorthand that allowed the audience to instantly clue in as to which character is on stage, as well as emphasize the emotions and expressions of the actor.
A ghost costume consisted of three main elements: * {{nihongo|White burial [[:en:Kimono|Kimono]]|[[:ja:白装束|白装束]]|shiro-shōzoku}} or {{nihongo||[[:ja:死に装束|死に装束]]|shini-shōzoku}}. This garment was also worn during {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Seppuku|Seppuku]]}}. *Wild, unkempt long black hair that often hides their face until they choose to reveal it. *Face make-up consisting of {{nihongo|white foundation||[[:en:oshiroi|oshiroi]]}} coupled with dramatic face painting ({{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Kumadori|Kumadori]]}}) of {{nihongo|blue shadows|藍隈|aiguma|extra2="[[:en:Indigo|Indigo]] fringe"}}, much like villains are depicted in kabuki make-up artistry.<ref>{{cite book|author=日本博学倶楽部|title=「通」になれる古典芸能を楽しむ本: 落語・歌舞伎から能・狂言まで|publisher=PHP研究所|year=2005|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZpY2LFHGK34C&pg=PT57|page=57|isbn=978-4569665498}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Parker|first=Helen S. E.|title=Progressive Traditions: An Illustrated Study of Plot Repetition In Traditional Japanese Theatre|publisher=BRILL|year=2006|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=L3pp4I-eoZIC&pg=PA87|page=87|isbn=978-9004145344}}</ref>{{efn|In addition to blue, {{nihongo|brown shadows|代赭隈|taishaguma|extra2="[[:en:red ochre|red ochre]] fringe"}} or black {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Kumadori|Kumadori]]}} ({{Harvnb|日本博学倶楽部|2005|p=57}}) are also used.}}

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ca:Onryō]][[de:Onryō]][[en:Onryō]][[es:Onryō]][[fa:اونریو]][[fr:Onryō]][[hu:Onrjó]][[id:Onryō]][[it:Onryō]][[ja:怨霊]][[jv:Onryō]][[ko:원령]][[mk:Онрјоо]][[ms:Onryō]][[nl:Onryo]][[no:Onryō]][[pl:Onryō]][[pt:Onryō]][[ru:Онрё]][[sc:Onryō]][[simple:Onryō]][[tr:Onryō]][[uk:Онрьо]][[vi:Onryō]][[zh:怨靈]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q634195]] Wikidata name: onryō [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 08:49, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{short description|Type of ghost in Japanese folklore}} {{for|the Japanese professional wrestler|Onryo (wrestler)}} {{Jmyth infobox}} {{Italic title}} [[File:Yoshitsuya The Lightning Bolt.jpg|thumb|{{transliteration|ja|[[Ukiyo-e]]}} by [[:en:Utagawa Yoshitsuya|Utagawa Yoshitsuya]] depicts the moment when [[:en:Emperor Sutoku|Emperor Sutoku]], who died in exile, became an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.]] [[File:Taira no Masakado Kubizuka.jpg|thumb|The headstone of [[:en:Taira no Masakado|Taira no Masakado]], located between the skyscrapers of [[:en:Ōtemachi|Ōtemachi]] near [[:en:Tokyo Station|Tokyo Station]], was renovated in 2021 when the surrounding skyscrapers were rebuilt, but the headstone was never moved.]] [[File:Tsukioka (Taiso) Yoshitoshi (1839-1892), Sugawara no Michizane roept een onweersbui op boven KyotoKôkoku (1880).jpg|thumb|{{transliteration|ja|Ukiyo-e}} by [[:en:Tsukioka Yoshitoshi|Tsukioka Yoshitoshi]] depicting [[:en:Sugawara no Michizane|Sugawara no Michizane]] as the {{nihongo3|{{transliteration|ja|[[kami]]}} of thunder||[[:en:Tenjin (kami)|Tenjin]]}}. After Sugawara no Michizane's death, lightning struck the palace, killing and injuring many of the powerful people involved in his banishment, and Sugawara no Michizane was enshrined in the {{transliteration|ja|[[Tenmangū]]}} ([[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]]) as the Tenjin.]] [[File:Hokusai Onryo.jpg|thumb|Onryō from the {{nihongo||近世怪談霜夜星|Kinsei-Kaidan-Shimoyonohoshi}}]]
In Japanese traditional beliefs and literature, {{nihongo3|{{lit|[[:en:Vengeful ghost|vengeful spirit]]}}, sometimes rendered "wrathful spirits", "hatred spirits", "resentful spirits", "ruthless spirits", "envious spirits", "dark spirits", "fallen spirits", or "downcast spirits"||'''onryō'''}}<ref name="grappard"/> are a type of ghost ({{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Yūrei|Yūrei]]}}) believed to be capable of causing harm in the world of the living, injuring or killing enemies, or even causing natural disasters to exact [[:en:revenge|vengeance]] to "redress" the wrongs it received while alive, then taking their spirits from their dying bodies. {{transliteration|ja|Onryō}} are often depicted as wronged women, who are traumatized, envious, disappointed, bitter, or just infuriated by what happened during life and exact revenge in death. These kinds of ghosts appear extremely vengeful, ruthless, heartless, brutal, cruel, deranged, egotistical, selfish, bloodthirsty, and cold-hearted.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lovelace |first=Ada |date=2008 |title=Ghostly and monstrous manifestations of women: Edo to contemporary |url=https://irishgothicjournal.net/issue5 |journal=The Irish Journal of Gothic and Horror Studies |issue=5 |page=30}}</ref>
[[:en:Emperor Sutoku|Emperor Sutoku]], [[:en:Taira no Masakado|Taira no Masakado]], and [[:en:Sugawara no Michizane|Sugawara no Michizane]] are called the {{nihongo|Three Great Onryō of Japan|[[:ja:日本三大怨霊|日本三大怨霊]]|Nihon Sandai Onryō}} because they are considered to be the most powerful and revered {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} in Japanese history. After they died with resentment and anger, there was a series of deaths of political opponents, natural disasters, and wars, and the rulers enshrined them as {{transliteration|ja|[[kami]]}} and deified them in [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]] to appease the resentment and anger that had turned them into {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://dot.asahi.com/dot/2019091300037.html?page=1|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210304044436/https://dot.asahi.com/dot/2019091300037.html?page=1|script-title=ja:崇徳天皇はなぜ「日本三大怨霊」の一人になったのか？ 悲劇の人生とは|language=ja|publisher=[[Asahi Shimbun]]|date=14 September 2019|archive-date=4 March 2021|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://thegate12.com/jp/article/351|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221103100624/https://thegate12.com/jp/article/351|script-title=ja:史上最恐！【日本三大怨霊】にまつわる悲しい歴史とは？ゆかりの場所も紹介|language=ja|publisher=The Gate|date=22 January 2021|archive-date=3 November 2022|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref>
{{transliteration|ja|Onryō}} are used as subjects in various traditional Japanese performing arts such as [[:en:Noh|Noh]], [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]], and [[Rakugo]]; for example, {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Hannya|Hannya]]}} is a Noh mask representing a female {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.<ref name="kurabayashi">{{cite book|pages=6, 7, 39|title=般若面を打つ 原寸型紙と詳細なプロセス写真で学ぶ|author=Akira Kurabayashi|publisher=Japan Publications, Inc.|year=2013|isbn=978-4817050823}}</ref>
The Japanese people's reverence for {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} has been passed down to the present day. {{nihongo|The head mound of Taira no Masakado|[[:ja:将門塚|将門塚]]|Masakado-zuka or Shōmon-zuka}}, located between skyscrapers near [[:en:Tokyo Station|Tokyo Station]], was to be moved several times as part of urban redevelopment projects, but each move resulted in the death of a construction worker and a series of accidents. Although the buildings surrounding the Taira no Masakado mound have been rebuilt many times, the mound has remained intact between the high-rise buildings. Even today, the mound is carefully maintained.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://president.jp/articles/-/37926?page=2|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210928235755/https://president.jp/articles/-/37926?page=2|script-title=ja:地価40億円の超一等地｢Taira no Masakadoの首塚｣が再開発を免れているホラーな理由|language=ja|publisher=President Online|date=14 August 2022|archive-date=28 September 2021|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref>
The term {{nihongo||[[Wiktionary:御霊|御霊]]|[[goryō]]}} is often used as a synonym for {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}, but the term {{transliteration|ja|goryō}} is more commonly used to refer to the {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} that have become the object of the people's reverence after a noble person has died a politically unjust death. {{nihongo3||[[:ja:御霊信仰|御霊信仰]]|Goryō Shinko}} refers to the belief that the {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} of people who have died unfortunate deaths cause hauntings and disasters, and the belief that they are enshrined as {{transliteration|ja|kami}} to appease them.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%BE%A1%E9%9C%8A%E4%BF%A1%E4%BB%B0-66557|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230206025148/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%BE%A1%E9%9C%8A%E4%BF%A1%E4%BB%B0-66557|script-title=ja:御霊信仰|language=ja|publisher=Kotobank|archive-date=6 February 2023|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%BE%A1%E9%9C%8A-505236|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230206025142/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%BE%A1%E9%9C%8A-505236|script-title=ja:御霊|language=ja|publisher=Kotobank|archive-date=6 February 2023|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%80%A8%E9%9C%8A-42048|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230206025148/https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%80%A8%E9%9C%8A-42048|script-title=ja:怨霊|language=ja|publisher=Kotobank|archive-date=6 February 2023|access-date=24 February 2023}}</ref>
==Origin== While the origin of {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} is unclear, belief in their existence can be traced back to the 8th century and was based on the idea that powerful and enraged souls of the dead could influence, harm, and kill the living. The earliest {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} cult that developed was around [[:en:Prince Naga|Prince Naga]] who died in 729;<ref name="grappard"/> and the first record of possession by the {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} spirit affecting health is found in the chronicle {{transliteration|ja|[[Shoku Nihongi]]}} (797), which states that "{{nihongo|[[Fujiwara Hirotsugu]]|[[:ja:藤原広嗣|藤原広嗣]]}}'s soul harmed [[:en:Genbō|Genbō]] to death" (Hirotsugu having died in a failed insurrection, named the "[[:en:Fujiwara no Hirotsugu Rebellion|Fujiwara no Hirotsugu Rebellion]]", after failing to remove his rival, the priest Genbō, from power).<ref>{{Harvnb|Suzuki|2011|loc=135 (note 2 to Chapter 2)}}</ref><ref>{{Harvnb|McCullough|1973|p=97}}</ref>
==Vengeance== According to the belief of [[:en:Ikiryō|Ikiryō]], a person's soul or spirit exists naturally when it is stable or in balance. When too much hatred or resentment brews, it can become separated from the body, resulting in the spirit becoming an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}. This can allegedly also occur in individuals who died an untimely death.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Yamada |first1=Yuji |title=怨霊とは何か (What is [an] Onryo) |publisher=Chuokoron-Shinsha |location=Japan |url=https://www.kinokuniya.co.jp/f/dsg-01-9784121022813}}</ref>
Traditionally in Japan, {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} driven by [[:en:revenge|vengeance]] were thought capable of causing not only their enemy's death, as in the case of Hirotsugu's vengeful spirit held responsible for killing the priest [[:en:Genbō|Genbō]],<ref>{{citation|last=McCullough|first=William H.|title=Spirit Possession in the Heian Period|editor-last1=Ōta|editor-first1=Saburo (太田三郎)|editor-last2=Fukuda|editor-first2=Rikutaro (福田陸太郎)|journal=Studies on Japanese Culture (日本文化研究論集)|volume=1|year=1973|page=97|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qLAdAQAAMAAJ}}; (Also printed in ''Nihon Bunka Kenkyū Kokusai Kaigi gijiroku'' (日本文化研究国際会議議事錄) ([https://books.google.com/books?id=RN9YAAAAMAAJ Volume 1, 1973], pp. 350- (p.356)</ref> but causing natural disasters such as [[:en:Earthquake|Earthquake]]s, [[:en:Fire|Fire]]s, [[:en:Storm|Storm]]s, [[:en:Drought|Drought]], [[:en:Famine|Famine]] and [[:en:Pandemic|pestilence]],<ref name="grappard"/> as in the case of [[:en:Prince Sawara|Prince Sawara]]'s spirit embittered against his brother, the [[Emperor Kanmu]].<ref name="suzuki">{{cite book|last=Suzuki|first=Yui|title=Medicine Master Buddha: The Iconic Worship of Yakushi in Heian Japan|publisher=BRILL|year=2011|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dgo7JV9vNCQC&pg=PA29|pages=29–31|isbn=978-9004196018}}</ref> In common parlance, such vengeance exacted by supernatural beings or forces is termed {{nihongo||[[:ja:祟り|祟り]]|tatari}}.<ref name="grappard">{{citation|last=Grappard|first=Allan G.|contribution=Religious practices|editor-last=Hall|editor-first=John Whitney|volume=2|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eiTWWfoyuyAC&pg=PA560|pages=559–|isbn=978-0521223539|title=The Cambridge History of Japan|year=1988|publisher=Cambridge University Press }}</ref>
The [[Emperor Kanmu]] had accused his brother Sawara, possibly falsely, of plotting to remove him from the throne. Sawara was then exiled, and died by fasting. According to a number of scholars, the reason that the Emperor moved the capital to [[Nagaoka-kyō]] thence to [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]] was an attempt to avoid the wrath of his brother's spirit, according to a number of scholars.<ref name="suzuki"/> This not succeeding entirely, the emperor tried to lift the curse by appeasing his brother's ghost, by performing Buddhist rites to pay respect, and granting Prince Sawara the posthumous title of emperor.<ref name="suzuki"/>
A well-known example of appeasement of the {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} spirit is the case of [[:en:Sugawara no Michizane|Sugawara no Michizane]], who had been politically disgraced and died in exile. It was believed to cause the death of his calumniators in quick succession, as well as catastrophes (especially lightning damage), and the court tried to appease the wrathful spirit by restoring Michizane's old Rank and position.<ref name="grappard"/> Michizane became deified in the cult of the [[:en:Tenjin (kami)|Tenjin]], with [[Tenmangū|Tenman-gū]] shrines erected around him.
===Examples=== Possibly the most famous {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} is Oiwa, from the {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Yotsuya Kaidan|Yotsuya Kaidan]]}}. In this story the husband remains unharmed; however, he is the target of the {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}'s vengeance. Oiwa's vengeance on him is not physical retribution, but rather psychological torment.
Other examples include:
; How a Man's Wife Became a Vengeful Ghost and How Her Malignity Was Diverted by a Master of Divination : In this tale from the medieval collection {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Konjaku Monogatarishū|Konjaku Monogatarishū]]}}, an abandoned wife is found dead with a full head of hair intact and her bones still attached. The husband, fearing retribution from her spirit, asks a [[Onmyōji|diviner]] for aid. The husband must endure while grabbing her hair and riding astride her corpse. She complains of the heavy load and leaves the house to "go looking" (presumably for her husband), but after a day she gives up and returns, after which the diviner is able to complete her exorcism with an incantation.<ref>{{cite book|translator-last=Jones|translator-first=S. W.|title=Ages ago; thirty-seven tales from the Konjaku monogatari collection|publisher=[[Harvard University Press]]|location=Cambridge, Massachusetts|year=1959|page=72|isbn=9780674181366 |format=snippet|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nv-wAAAAIAAJ}}</ref><ref>One of the texts cited by Jones: {{citation|editor-last=Haga|editor-first=Yaichi (芳賀矢一)|script-chapter=ja:卷第廿四/第20: 人妻成悪靈除其害陰陽師語 |script-title=ja:攷証今昔物語集 |title=Kōshō konjaku monogatari shū |volume=3 |year=1921 |page=106 |url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/945416}}</ref> ; Of a Promise Broken : In this tale from the [[:en:Izumo Province|Izumo]] area recorded by [[:en:Lafcadio Hearn|Lafcadio Hearn]], a [[:en:Samurai|Samurai]] vows to his dying wife never to remarry. He soon breaks this promise, and the ghost of the deceased wife murders her husband's new young bride, ripping her head off. A watchman chases down the apparition, and, while slashing his sword, recites a [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] prayer, destroying the ghost of the dead wife.<ref>{{citation|last=Hearn|first=Lafcadio|chapter=Of a Promise Broken|publisher=Little, Brown|year=1901|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DGEiAAAAMAAJ&pg=PA15|pages=15–26|title=A Japanese miscellany}}</ref>
==In media==
The {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} is a staple of the [[:en:J-Horror|J-Horror genre]], most notable being [[:en:Sadako Yamamura|Sadako Yamamura]] and [[:en:Kayako Saeki|Kayako Saeki]] from the ''[[:en:The Ring (franchise)|Ring]]'' and ''[[:en:Ju-On (franchise)|Ju-On]]'' franchises, respectively. The characters in these works are almost exclusively women who were wronged in life and returned as {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} to wreak havoc on the living and obtain revenge.<ref>{{Cite web|last=O'Sullivan|first=Dan|date=2020-10-27|title=Japan's Onryō Spirits Inhabit a Purgatory of Revenge and Cosmic Rage|url=http://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/monster-mythology-onryo|access-date=2021-05-04|website=Atlas Obscura|language=en}}</ref>
In ''[[:en:The Ring (franchise)|The Ring]]'' [[:en:Sadako Yamamura|Sadako Yamamura]] is the main antagonist. Her origin is from the ''Ring'' novel series by [[:en:Koji Suzuki|Koji Suzuki]], where she haunts and kills people through tapes on a TV. Before her death she is raped by a doctor with smallpox, who seals her in a well where she dies. Before Sadako dies she promises to take revenge on the world, and becomes an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.
The aforementioned {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Yotsuya Kaidan|Yotsuya Kaidan]]}} has been made into numerous movies and retold many times over the course of Japanese history. The story revolves around Tamiya Iemon and his wife Oiwa. Their relationship is not a happy one, and through some set of circumstances Iemon gives Oiwa a powder that permanently disfigures her face. Upon realizing this Oiwa takes her own life and that of her baby. After her death she comes back to haunt Iemon and his new wife, becoming an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.<ref>{{Cite book |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JR9JAAAAQBAJ&pg=PA168 |chapter=Epic Yotsuya Ghost Tale |author=Tsuruya Nanboku IV |title=An Edo Anthology: Literature from Japan's Mega-City, 1750-1850 |orig-date=1825 |date=2013 |publisher=[[University of Hawaiʻi Press]] |editor1=Sumie Jones |editor2=Kenji Watanabe |isbn=978-0-8248-3776-1 |oclc=859157616 |pages=168–182}}</ref>
{{transliteration|ja|[[Banchō Sarayashiki]]}} is another Japanese ghost story that has been retold many ways. In this story Okiku, a beautiful maid, is the target of desire for the samurai whose house she works at, Aoyama Tessan. She continually refuses his advances, and in a fit of rage Tessan hides one of 10 expensive plates that Okiku is in charge of counting. When Okiku cannot find the 10th plate she recounts them obsessively, panicking more each time. Tessan tells her he will forgive her losing the plate if she becomes his mistress, but even then she refuses him. At her refusal Tessan throws her into a well on the property, where she dies. After this, every night Okiku rises from the well, softly counting to 9, and then letting out a horrendous shriek once she reaches 10. She has become an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Kaidan of Bancho Sarayashiki The Dish Mansion at Bancho |url=https://www.grimoireofhorror.com/the-yurei/kaidan-bancho-sarayashiki/ |access-date=2022-04-11 |website=Grimoire of Horror |date=11 January 2021 |language=en-US}}</ref>
{{nihongo|[[List of Killer Instinct characters#Hisako|Hisako]]|久子||extra= "Eternal Child" or "Everlasting Child"}}, from the third entry of the fighting game ''[[:en:Killer Instinct|Killer Instinct]]'', is an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} who died while defending her village. She still haunts her old village and will take vengeance on anyone who desecrates its ruins with her {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Naginata|Naginata]]}}. She has pale white skin and long black hair like most {{transliteration|ja|onryō}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ultra-combo.com/characters/hisako/|title = Hisako|date = 12 December 2016}}</ref>
In 2018, the asymmetrical horror game ''[[:en:Dead by Daylight|Dead by Daylight]]'' released the ''Shattered Bloodline'' chapter DLC, and with it came Rin Yamaoka, The Spirit. The Spirit is an {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} who returns from the dead after being brutally murdered by her father.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Shattered Bloodline - Dead by Daylight|url=http://deadbydaylight.com/en/chapters/shattered-bloodline|access-date=2021-05-04|website=deadbydaylight.com|language=en}}</ref> In March 2022, Sadako Yamamura was added as a playable character.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sea.ign.com/dead-by-daylight/182036/news/dead-by-daylight-x-ringu-crossover-revealed|title = Dead by Daylight x Ringu Crossover Revealed|date = 15 February 2022}}</ref>
The term {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} is also present in the game ''[[:en:Phasmophobia (video game)|Phasmophobia]]''. It is one of 24 ghost types that the player can identify, and is noted for treating lit candles like a crucifix.
Yoshie Kimura, the main antagonist from ''[[Death Forest]]'', is an Onryō. She died when exploring the forest with her classmate, from being beaten to death by an unknown person.
Mizu, the protagonist of the 2023 [[:en:Netflix|Netflix]] series ''[[:en:Blue Eye Samurai|Blue Eye Samurai]]'' shares many similarities with, and is often compared diegetically to, an Onryō.
==Physical appearance== Traditionally, {{transliteration|ja|onryō}} and other {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Yūrei|Yūrei]]}} (ghosts) had no particular appearance. However, with the rising of popularity of [[:en:Kabuki|Kabuki]] during the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]], a specific [[:en:costume|costume]] was developed.
Highly visual in nature, and with a single actor often assuming various roles within a play, kabuki developed a system of visual shorthand that allowed the audience to instantly clue in as to which character is on stage, as well as emphasize the emotions and expressions of the actor.
A ghost costume consisted of three main elements: * {{nihongo|White burial [[:en:Kimono|Kimono]]|[[:ja:白装束|白装束]]|shiro-shōzoku}} or {{nihongo||[[:ja:死に装束|死に装束]]|shini-shōzoku}}. This garment was also worn during {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Seppuku|Seppuku]]}}. *Wild, unkempt long black hair that often hides their face until they choose to reveal it. *Face make-up consisting of {{nihongo|white foundation||[[:en:oshiroi|oshiroi]]}} coupled with dramatic face painting ({{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Kumadori|Kumadori]]}}) of {{nihongo|blue shadows|藍隈|aiguma|extra2="[[:en:Indigo|Indigo]] fringe"}}, much like villains are depicted in kabuki make-up artistry.<ref>{{cite book|author=日本博学倶楽部|title=「通」になれる古典芸能を楽しむ本: 落語・歌舞伎から能・狂言まで|publisher=PHP研究所|year=2005|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZpY2LFHGK34C&pg=PT57|page=57|isbn=978-4569665498}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Parker|first=Helen S. E.|title=Progressive Traditions: An Illustrated Study of Plot Repetition In Traditional Japanese Theatre|publisher=BRILL|year=2006|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=L3pp4I-eoZIC&pg=PA87|page=87|isbn=978-9004145344}}</ref>{{efn|In addition to blue, {{nihongo|brown shadows|代赭隈|taishaguma|extra2="[[:en:red ochre|red ochre]] fringe"}} or black {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Kumadori|Kumadori]]}} ({{Harvnb|日本博学倶楽部|2005|p=57}}) are also used.}}
